name: SRI LANKA
lead: Sri Lanka is a teardrop island off the tip of India. It has ancient temples, misty tea hills, golden beaches, and wild elephants. People have called it the Pearl of the Indian Ocean for 2,000 years.
geo: Sri Lanka sits in the Indian Ocean, just 31 km from India's southern tip. Cool, cloudy highlands fill the centre. Waterfalls tumble past tea farms.
Flat plains wrap around the highlands. The south-west gets heavy monsoon rain. The north-east stays dry.
animals: Wild Asian elephants roam the ancient forests. Blue whales, the biggest animals on Earth, swim off the south coast from November to April.
Five of the world's seven sea turtle species nest on Sri Lanka's beaches. The Sri Lankan junglefowl, a bright bird, lives nowhere else on Earth.
culture: About 70% of Sri Lankans are Buddhist. Golden-roofed temples called viharas stand in every town. A famous temple in Kandy keeps the Buddha's Tooth Relic, the most sacred object in the country.
Tamil Hindus in the north hold fire-walking festivals. Everyone eats rice and curry with their fingers. The world's finest cinnamon was traded here 3,000 years ago.
history: People have lived here for at least 30,000 years. The Sinhalese kingdom of Anuradhapura ruled for over 1,000 years. Its builders dug huge tanks to store water for rice.
Arab, Portuguese, Dutch, and British traders all wanted Sri Lanka's spices, gems, and harbours. Britain called it Ceylon. It gained independence in 1948 and became Sri Lanka in 1972.
wows: Cinnamon grew wild here and reached Egypt over 3,000 years ago.
Sapphires and rubies wash out of riverbeds after rain.
Sri Lanka elected the world's first female prime minister in 1960.
Blue whales sometimes swim close enough to spot from the beach.
Sigiriya fortress, built in the 5th century, sits on a 180-metre rock.
The word 'serendipity' comes from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka.
Buddhist, Hindu, Muslim, and Christian pilgrims all climb Adam's Peak.

myths.myth: Sri Lanka has always grown tea
myths.fact: Coffee came first. A plant disease killed the coffee farms in the 1800s, so farmers planted tea.
Cinnamon is bark. Workers peel it from young shoots, and it curls into sticks as it dries.
